pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 5–6 (Reception/Year 1). COUNTING OBJECTS TO 20 — applying one-to-one correspondence AND cardinality to answer 'how many?' for sets up to 20 in any arrangement (line, array, circle, scattered), and counting out a given number (give-N). Where the counting principles become a reliable procedure.
• Standards — UK (DfE): NC Year 1 'count, read and write numbers to 100 in numerals' and 'read and write numbers from 1 to 20 in numerals and words'. Underpinned by EYFS object counting; teen numbers (11–19) as 'ten and some more' bridge to place value.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.CC.5 verbatim — 'Count to answer "how many?" questions about as many as 20 things arranged in a line, a rectangular array, or a circle, or as many as 10 things in a scattered configuration; given a number from 1–20, count out that many objects.'
• Operational details: Combine one-to-one (tag each once) with cardinality (last word = total). Arrangement matters: line/array/circle are easier (a natural order exists); SCATTERED is hardest — the child must impose tracking (move counted items aside, or count round systematically). Give-N (count out exactly N) is the stronger check. Use the TEN-FRAME so teens read as a full ten + extras ('ten and three' = 13), seeding place value.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (5) counts a line of up to 20 accurately and counts ≤10 scattered by organising them. Tier B (5–6) counts 20 in any arrangement and gives-N up to 20. Tier C (6) counts a scattered 20 with a self-chosen tracking strategy and reads a teen set on a ten-frame as 'ten and __'.
bestPractices: Insist on a tracking strategy for scattered sets — move each counted object aside, or count along a consistent path — so nothing is missed or double-counted.
Use give-N ('count out 13') as the strongest assessment — harder than 'how many?' and it exposes shaky cardinality.
Introduce the ten-frame for teens: fill a ten, then extras, so 14 is seen as 'ten and four' (early place value, not a mystery word).
Vary the arrangement deliberately (line → array → circle → scattered) so counting is robust to layout and the 'different arrangement = different number' error is defeated.
Keep objects moveable and connect the count to the written numeral and the spoken 'altogether'.
keyRepresentations: Ten-frames (one full + a partial for teens).
Sets shown in line / array / circle / scattered (a deliberate arrangement ladder).
A numeral card matched to the counted set.
commonMisconceptions: Losing track on scattered sets → skips or double-counts (no tracking strategy).
Recounting when asked 'how many?' (cardinality not secure) or miscounting across the teens.
Treating teen numbers as unanalysable words rather than 'ten and some ones'.
Believing a rearranged set has a different total (conservation).

learn.summary: Ages 5–6 (Reception/Year 1) counting objects to 20: coordinating one-to-one correspondence (tag each item exactly once) with cardinality (the last count word is the total) to answer 'how many?' for sets in any arrangement — line, array, circle, or scattered — and to count out a given number (give-N). Scattered sets are hardest because the child must impose a tracking strategy; give-N is the strongest check of cardinality. Ten-frames help teen numbers read as 'ten and some more', seeding place value. (The cited standard specifies scattered configurations up to 10 and ordered arrangements up to 20.)

activities.title: Organise and count a scattered set
feedback: If repeat counts give different totals, something went wrong in at least one count. Often counted and uncounted items got mixed up, but a number word may also have been skipped, or the words and pointing may have got out of step. Listen to the number sequence, and try physically moving each one aside as you count: 'move each one over here as you count it.'
If asked 'how many?' and the child recounts from the start, prompt: 'You just counted — what was the last number? That tells us how many.'
Ask: 'How could you count the scattered ones so you don't lose your place?' to prompt a self-chosen strategy rather than supplying one every time.
Rearrange the same counters and ask how many now — the total should not change because nothing was added or removed.
activities.rationale: One-to-one and cardinal principles must be coordinated to enumerate reliably, and moveable objects let a child physically track counted versus uncounted. Scattered arrangements demand a self-imposed strategy, which develops with practice rather than reteaching the count. The standard specifies scattered sets to 10; counting ~20 scattered is a harder extension drawn from the original Tier C.
sourceClaims: K.CC.5 verbatim: 'Count to answer "how many?" questions about as many as 20 things arranged in a line, a rectangular array, or a circle, or as many as 10 things in a scattered configuration; given a number from 1–20, count out that many objects.'
One-one plus cardinal principles must be coordinated to reliably enumerate a set; tangible moveable objects help track counted vs uncounted.
learnerActions: Start with a small scattered pile (up to 10) of moveable counters or buttons spread randomly.
Count them by moving each counted item aside into a 'counted' tray (or sliding it along a consistent path) so counted and uncounted are clearly separated.
Say how many there are altogether, then recount and check you get the same number.
Repeat with a larger scattered set of up to 20 counters (a harder extension), choosing your own tracking path.
Match a numeral card to the final count.
activities.intendedInsight: A chaotic scatter becomes reliably countable by imposing order — moving each item as you count it so nothing is skipped or counted twice — and the last number you say is how many there are, no matter how the objects are arranged.

activities.title: Count out exactly N (give-N)
feedback: If the child counts past the target or hands over the whole pile, they are not yet using the number as a stop signal — state the target, count into a cupped hand, and do a stop-and-check: 'how many do we need? tell me when to stop.'
Follow up with 'Give me 4 more — now how many?' to link counting-on to the running total.
Praise stopping at exactly the right item, not just producing counters.
activities.rationale: Give-N is harder than 'how many?' because it requires holding a target while counting; it exposes shaky cardinality that a plain count can hide. Stopping at the target rebuilds the last-word-as-total link.
sourceClaims: K.CC.5 verbatim: 'Count to answer "how many?" questions about as many as 20 things arranged in a line, a rectangular array, or a circle, or as many as 10 things in a scattered configuration; given a number from 1–20, count out that many objects.'
learnerActions: From a large pile, count out exactly a requested number (e.g. 'give me 13') into a cupped hand or small tray.
Say the target first, then count one item at a time, stopping when you reach it.
Check: 'How many did we need? Tell me when to stop' — point and count together to confirm you stopped at the target.
Try a round with a teen target such as 16, then compare counting out from different-sized piles.
activities.intendedInsight: Counting out a specific quantity means using the target number as a stop signal — you hold the goal in mind while counting, which is cardinality in action and a stronger test than simply reporting 'how many'.

activities.title: Vary the arrangement to make counting robust
feedback: If a child expects a different total after rearranging, slowly rearrange in front of them and recount together: nothing was added or taken away, so it stays the same.
Ask: 'If you started counting the line from the other end, how many?' to challenge the idea that direction changes the total.

Lines and arrays have a natural order to follow. Circles have an order too, but no natural start or end, so the child must mark or remember where they began to avoid counting items twice. Scattered sets need a strategy the child imposes. Name these differences so the child knows when extra care is needed.
activities.rationale: Deliberately varying arrangement makes counting robust to layout and challenges the belief that a different arrangement means a different number. Lines and arrays offer a natural order. A circle offers an order but no natural starting point, so the start must be marked. Scattered sets require imposed tracking. The conservation point — same total after rearranging — is a reasonable curricular inference and is not directly asserted by the cited standard.
sourceClaims: K.CC.5 verbatim: 'Count to answer "how many?" questions about as many as 20 things arranged in a line, a rectangular array, or a circle, or as many as 10 things in a scattered configuration; given a number from 1–20, count out that many objects.'
learnerActions: Count the same quantity shown four ways in turn: a line, a rectangular array, a circle, and scattered.
After counting a neat line, count it again starting from the other end and check the total is the same.
Count an array along rows, then along columns, and confirm the total does not change.
State each total aloud with 'altogether' and match it to the written numeral.
activities.intendedInsight: The total depends only on the objects, not on how they are laid out or which end you start from — a rearranged set still has the same number.

activities.title: Read teen numbers on a ten-frame as 'ten and some more'
feedback: If a teen is treated as an unanalysable word, point to the full frame and the extras: 'a full ten, and three more — thirteen.'
If the count across the teens slips, slow down and fill one frame completely before starting the extras.
Connect the spoken 'ten and four', the filled ten-frame, and the numeral 14 so all three line up.
activities.rationale: Ten-frames show teen numbers as ten-and-ones, which seeds place value and helps a child stop treating teens as random words. Note: the ten-frame source for this claim is marked unverified in the row and was not re-verified in this rewrite.
sourceClaims: Ten-frames represent teen numbers as ten-and-ones, seeding place value.
learnerActions: Count a teen quantity (11–19) by filling a ten-frame completely first, then placing the extras in a second frame.
Say the number as 'ten and three… thirteen' so the full ten and the extras are both visible.
Match the ten-frame picture to the written numeral (e.g. 13).
Repeat with other teen numbers, each time noticing the full ten plus a few more.
activities.intendedInsight: A teen number is not a mysterious word — it is a full ten with a few more ones, which is the beginning of place value.

activities.title: Spot and fix a miscount (optional Socratic check)
feedback: If the child misses the error, slow the demonstration down and point at the item that was skipped or double-counted.
Encourage them to name the fix ('move each one over as you count') rather than only saying 'it's wrong'.
activities.rationale: Fixing another's miscount may have mild Socratic value for articulating counting principles, but the core skill is an enacted count, so this supplements rather than replaces hands-on counting. Its efficacy is proposed, not validated.
sourceClaims: One-one plus cardinal principles must be coordinated to reliably enumerate a set; tangible moveable objects help track counted vs uncounted.
learnerActions: Watch (or listen to) a puppet or partner count a scattered pile, deliberately skipping one item or counting one twice.
Decide whether the count was right, explain what went wrong, and show how to count it correctly using a tracking strategy.
Suggest what the puppet should do differently next time (e.g. move each item aside).
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to catch and explain a counting slip shows you understand why one-to-one tagging and tracking matter — not just how to recite numbers.

constraints: The core objective is an enacted count: the child must physically tag, track, and count out objects. Recognition-only tasks (choosing 'how many?' from options, judging a shown count) can assess or supplement but do not by themselves elicit the independent counting and give-N that is the point.
A labelled, already-counted set can serve as a reference example but cannot enact the count or the give-N task; use it only as a scaffold.
Give-N (count out exactly N) is a stronger check of cardinality than 'how many?' — include it, not just set-reporting.
Scattered-set tracking is a developing habit: if a child loses track, model a strategy (move each item aside) rather than reteaching counting as though the concept is absent.
Keep objects moveable and connect each count to the spoken total ('altogether') and the written numeral.

If an on-screen version is used, features like tap-to-count lockout (a counted item cannot be tapped again), a 'tidy into a line/ten-frame' helper, a drag-out give-N mode, and a persistent total badge can make the mechanism concrete — these are optional illustrations, not required mechanisms, and should not replace hands-on counting with physical objects.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved research row without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The ten-frame/place-value source (NCETM early number guidance) is marked verified:false in the row; its claim is used cautiously and the uncertainty is noted in the ten-frame activity.
The conservation point in the arrangement-variation activity (rearranged set has the same total) is a reasonable curricular inference but is not directly asserted by any cited source claim.

The cited K.CC.5 standard specifies scattered configurations up to 10 and ordered arrangements (line/array/circle) up to 20. Activity 1's scattered set of up to 20 is a harder extension carried over from the original row's Tier C checkpoint, not a standard requirement.
The original prerequisite links (e.g. for point/say coordination and count-out overrun) are assessment-row metadata not reproduced as learner-facing content; retained conceptually as feedback moves.
No arithmetic or conceptual errors were found in the source counting examples (13 as a full ten plus three, 14 as 'ten and four', 17 in a line, counting out 16); these were preserved as given.

probeDeeper: How many did you get? Count them again — do you get the same?
How could you count the scattered ones so you don't lose your place?
Give me 4 more — now how many?
If you started counting the line from the other end, how many?
assess.correctAnswer: Tags each object once, keeps track of counted versus uncounted in the scattered set (moving or organising them), answers 'how many' with the last count word, and stops at exactly 13 when counting out.

errorPatterns.pattern: loses track on scattered sets — recounts or skips objects because counted and uncounted aren't separated
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT reteach counting as if the concept were missing — model a strategy: 'move each one over here as you count it', which is a tracking habit that develops with practice
errorPatterns.revealedBy: different totals on repeat counts of the scattered set; no strategy to keep place

errorPatterns.pattern: point/say coordination slip — number words come faster or slower than the pointing, so tags don't line up one-to-one
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT drill — slow to one touch per word, sliding each item aside; the coordination tightens with the move-it scaffold
errorPatterns.revealedBy: fingers and words out of sync, giving an over- or under-count

errorPatterns.pattern: count-out overrun — asked for exactly 13, counts past it or hands over the whole pile; doesn't use 13 as a stop signal
errorPatterns.nextMove: state the target, count into a cupped hand, and stop-and-check — 'how many do we need? tell me when to stop'; this rebuilds the last-word-as-total link
errorPatterns.revealedBy: keeps counting beyond 13 or gives all the counters

responseLevels.gap: Miscounts through skipping or double-counting, especially when scattered; cannot count out a requested quantity (keeps going past it).
responseLevels.full: Counts lines and scattered sets to 20 accurately with a tracking strategy, and counts out an exact requested quantity, stopping at the target.
responseLevels.partial: Counts a neat line to 20 accurately but loses track on scattered sets, or counts out a target only with support — the tracking strategy is not yet automatic.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are 17 counters in a line — count them and tell me how many. Now here are 10 counters scattered on the table — count these. Last, here's a big pile: count out exactly 13 for me. (Watch the one-to-one tagging, whether they organise the scattered set, and whether they stop at 13.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A neat line hides what the scattered set and the count-out reveal. The line tests tagging; the scattered set tests keeping track (the child must impose order or move items); counting out exactly 13 tests holding a target while counting (cardinality in action). A child weak in one-to-one double-counts or skips especially when scattered; a child weak in cardinality counts out but doesn't stop at 13.
